newsitem.title: USA: Upbeat G7 sees faster world economic growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Upbeat G7 sees faster world economic growth in 1997.

text.p: The Group of Seven richest industrial nations delivered an upbeat outlook for the world economy on Saturday, saying inflation was low and forecasting faster growth into 1997.
Top finance officials from the seven powerful nations also discussed ways of spreading the better times they see ahead to poorer countries by easing their debt burden.
In a statement issued after a nearly six-hour meeting, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the Group of Seven welcomed recent movements in currency markets.

"We welcomed developments in exchange markets over the recent period," Rubin, who acted as chairman of the meeting, said in his statement. "And we reaffirmed our standing commitment to reduce (trade) imbalances and to cooperate closely in the exchange markets."
The dollar has been buoyant in recent days, although currency rates have been broadly stable for some time.

Rubin said the G7 finance ministers and central bankers, gathered during the IMF and World bank annual meetings, believed the world economy had improved since they last met in April and looked forward to even better times ahead.

"The general sense around the table was that the outlook had improved since our last meeting and that conditions appear to be in place for a strengthening and broadening of the expansion of the world economy into 1997," Rubin said.
He said the G7 would seek to reduce government budget deficits in the medium term, pursue anti-inflationary policies and strengthen economic reforms.
"Throughout the G7 countries, inflation remains at low levels, efforts are underway to reduce fiscal deficits and external imbalances have receded," the Treasury chief said.
The G7 is comprised of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
With discussions freed of the acrimony that has sometimes characterised talks in the past, the G7 officials were able to focus on how to aid the world's poorest debtor nations.

Rubin said the Paris Club of creditor nations would sharply increase the amount of help they are prepared to offer the world's poorest debtor nations. Under the new initiative, up to 80 percent of their debts would be forgiven, compared with a 67 percent ceiling now.

The debt-relief initiative -- involving actions by the Paris Club of creditor countries, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank -- is aimed at putting debt-ridden poor nations, many of them in Africa, back on their feet.

"I hope we will be able to have the first countries to benefit from (the debt initiative)...before the end of the year," Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke told reporters after the G7 meeting.
